## Approach
Two pointers, one from each end, moving inward. I skip any character that isn't an ASCII letter or digit, compare the rest case-insensitively, and stop when the pointers cross. That gives linear time and constant extra space, no cleaned copy of the string.

## Code
```python
def is_palindrome(s):
    i, j = 0, len(s) - 1
    while i < j:
        while i < j and not s[i].isalnum():
            i += 1
        while i < j and not s[j].isalnum():
            j -= 1
        if s[i].lower() != s[j].lower():
            return False
        i += 1
        j -= 1
    return True
```

## Complexity
Time O(n), each character is visited at most once by the two pointers. Space O(1), only the two indices.

A read-write lock pays off when reads dominate and the critical section is long enough that serializing readers actually costs you. If most operations only read shared state, letting them run concurrently while writers stay exclusive buys real throughput. A plain mutex is the better call when writes are frequent, when the critical section is tiny, or when contention is low, because the extra bookkeeping and cache-line traffic of an RWMutex can make it slower than a simple lock. The rule of thumb I use is: reach for the read-write lock only when reads clearly outnumber writes and you can measure the win.

A read-write lock pays off when reads dominate and the critical section is long enough that serializing readers actually costs you. With a mutex, every reader blocks every other reader, so if you have many concurrent readers and rare writes, an RWMutex lets them proceed in parallel and only the writer takes exclusive access. The classic case is a cache or config map that's read on every request and updated occasionally.

It's not worth it when writes are frequent, because the writer still needs exclusivity and the reader-writer bookkeeping adds overhead on top of the lock itself. It's also not worth it when the critical section is tiny, since the lock cost dominates and a plain mutex is simpler and often faster. And if you're on a single core, or the read section is short, the parallelism buys you nothing. One more caveat: RWMutex readers can starve writers under heavy read load, so if write latency matters you need to think about that.
